title: Introduction: Why AI Products Need Stronger Guardrails
text: Hello, I'm Vinay Kumar Serawat. Normal software does what its code says, and an AI product is what it predicts, and that can be wrong, unsafe, or surprising. So, AI products need stronger guardrails. Here's what product managers should put in place. An AI product is safe when it resists misuse and survives mistakes. Normal software is predictable. A model is not, so safety has to be designed around it, tested, and watched after launch. Here are the six guardrails: hallucination controls, content safety, permissions, privacy, human approval, and transparency. Each one limits a different way the product can go wrong.

title: The 6 Core Guardrails for AI Safety
text: Hallucination controls reduce confident wrong answers, ground answers in trusted sources, ask for citations, and let the product say it does not know. Content safety filters harmful input and output, and it needs testing against people who try to bypass it. Neither control is perfect, so you layer them. Permissions decide what the AI can see and do. Give it the least access it needs, and make it respect each user's own rights, so it never shows one person another's data. Privacy means collecting less, protecting what you keep, and being clear about what is sent to model providers. Human approval puts a person in front of risky actions, like sending money, deleting data, or sending messages. Transparency tells users they are using AI, what it can and cannot do, and when it may be wrong. Together, they keep trust because people can see, check, and override. title: How AI Model Failures Differ from Traditional Software Bugs
text: In ways nobody predicted, on inputs nobody imagined, and attackers can steer it with plain language. That means more testing, more layers, and monitoring after launch, not only before. Responsible AI is a habit, not a banner. Assess risk before you build. Red team the product with people who try to break it. Write down what it should never do. Give users a way to report problems, and assign an owner who can pause the feature when something goes wrong. So, safety. Models are unpredictable, so add layers. title: Operationalizing Responsible AI: Red-Teaming & Kill-Switches
text: A product manager launching an AI feature that does this, describe it. List the top 10 ways it could cause harm or embarrassment, rate each by likelihood and severity, and propose one guardrail for each. Then tell me which action should always need human approval, and what I should say to users about its limits. Focus on the highest severity items first, a rare but serious harm usually deserves a guardrail before a common but minor one. Pause here and run it on your own product.
